On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reviewed several challenges: the sufficiency of the evidence supporting conviction, the admissibility of prior convictions under Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b), the admission of the detective’s testimony under Rule 704(b), and the court’s handling of the exhibits under Rule 403.
The Eighth Circuit held that sufficient evidence supported the jury’s findings as to intent and substantial step toward attempted receipt of child pornography. The court concluded the prior convictions were properly admitted for intent, motive, and knowledge, and were not unfairly prejudicial.

Brett Christian Kamerud A jury found Cory and Brett Kamerud guilty of conspiring to distribute and possessing with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of a mixture or substance containing a detectable amount of methamphetamine in violation of 21 U.S.C. §§ 841 (a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B), and 846. The jury also found one of the objects of the conspiracy was to possess the methamphetamine with the intent to distribute it to one or more persons under twenty-one years of age in violation of 21 U.S.C. § 859 .

 Brett also makes several of his own claims. First, he argues the district court plainly erred by failing to instruct the jury with Eighth Circuit Pattern Jury Instruction 506F, entitled “Conspiracy: Multiple Offenses.” 6 Brett argues the failure to use this particular instruction meant the jury did not understand it must unanimously agree upon one or more objects of the conspiracy to find him guilty. As we stated above, however, we are confident the jury fully understood they were required to unanimously find one or more of the objects of the conspiracy present before finding Brett guilty, because the verdict form shows the jury separately considered all four of the possible objects of the conspiracy, and did not unanimously agree upon one of the four. Furthermore, the district court gave a general unanimity instruction which provided “[y]ou should try to reach an agreement if you can do so without violence to individual judgment, because a verdict — whether guilty or not guilty — must be unanimous.” Under plain error review, we conclude the general unanimity instruction was sufficient to protect Brett’s constitutional rights.  See United States v. Gruenberg,  989 F.2d 971, 975 (8th Cir. 1993) (“A general unanimity instruction usually protects a defendant’s sixth amendment right to a unanimous verdict.”) (quoting  United States v. I.

Baker argues the evidence was insufficient to convict for the intent and substantial step elements of attempted receipt of child pornography.

This court reviews sufficiency of the evidence de novo, “viewing evidence in the light most favorable to the government, resolving conflicts in the government’s favor, and accepting all reasonable inferences that support the verdict.” United States v. Teague, 646 F.3d 1119, 1121–22 (8th Cir. 2011). This court upholds the verdict if “any interpretation of the evidence would allow a reasonable-minded jury to find the defendant guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.” Id. at 1122.

Baker argues the evidence shows only the intent to view adult pornography. His searches disprove this. He searched for terms like “young naked teen boys,” frequently focusing on the terms “boys,” or “young.” A reasonable jury could find that Baker narrowed his searches—sufficient evidence of intent to find child pornography.

As for the substantial step element, Baker had cache images on his devices of young-looking people engaging in sex acts. The ages of the (apparent) children in the cache images were unknown, but a reasonable jury could conclude they were child pornography. See United States v. Morrissey, 895 F.3d 541, 549 (8th Cir. 2018) (approving a jury finding that images were child pornography after viewing them). No. 02-2232, 02-2427.
United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit.
Submitted: Feb. 12, 2003.
Filed: April 23, 2003.

A jury found Cory and Brett Kamerud guilty of conspiring to distribute and possessing with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of a mixture or substance containing a detectable amount of methamphetamine in violation of 21 U.S.C. §§ 841(a)(1), 841(b)(1)(B), and 846. Background

At trial, the district court admitted Baker’s prior convictions for possession of child pornography and sexual exploitation of a minor. The court placed certain exhibits, including cached images, in a separate red binder subject to special handling procedures. Participants repeatedly called the contents “contraband,” but Baker did not object to the procedure or terminology.

The Eighth Circuit affirmed.
